Oration
o-RAY-shun
n. (a formal public speech; the last one Herod ever gave)
From Latin oratio, a speech, from orare, to speak or plead. The Authorized Version uses it once, of the address Herod made from his throne in royal apparel, after which he was smitten.

Biblical Definition

And upon a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration unto them. The people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man. And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost. Luke gives the whole sequence in three verses and the reason for the judgment in six words: because he gave not God the glory. The sin was not making the speech, nor the royal apparel, nor even the crowd's flattery, which Herod did not arrange. It was receiving what belonged to God and saying nothing. Compare Paul and Barnabas at Lystra, who rent their clothes and ran in among the people to stop precisely this, and Peter lifting Cornelius off the floor. Herod sat still. And then Luke sets the verse that always follows such a scene in Acts, with a deliberate contrast: But the word of God grew and multiplied. A king dies eaten of worms in one sentence, and the next sentence is about the thing that actually grows.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a speech or discourse composed according to the rules of oratory, and spoken in public; in Scripture, the address after which Herod was smitten for not giving God the glory.

expand to see more

ORATION, n. A speech or discourse composed according to the rules of oratory, and spoken in public.

ORATOR, n. A public speaker; in modern usage, a person of eloquence.

FLATTERY, n. False praise; commendation bestowed for the purpose of gaining favor and influence.

GLORY, n. Praise ascribed in adoration; honor; in Scripture, the exhibition of the divine perfections.

PRESUMPTION, n. Arrogance; blind or headstrong confidence; unreasonable adventurousness.

Key Scripture

Act 12:21 — "And upon a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration unto them."

Act 12:22 — "And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man."

Act 12:23 — "And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost."

Act 12:24 — "But the word of God grew and multiplied."

Modern Corruption

Receiving honour that belongs to God is treated as a failure of modesty rather than as theft; Luke records a death sentence executed on the spot, with the reason stated as giving not God the glory.

expand to see more

Acts 12 is arranged as a contrast and the arrangement is the argument. The chapter opens with Herod killing James with the sword and arresting Peter to please the people; it has the church praying and an angel opening an iron gate of its own accord; and it ends with the same king on a throne, receiving divine honours and struck down. Two men in prison, two very different outcomes, and one conclusion: But the word of God grew and multiplied. The kings of the earth set themselves against the Lord and against his anointed, and the book of Acts keeps noting quietly what happens to them and what happens to the word.

The sin named is precise and it is worth naming precisely, because the modern version is usually gentler than a throne and royal apparel. A man receives credit he knows is not his and does not correct it. A ministry accepts a reputation it has not earned. A leader lets an impression stand because contradicting it would cost something. Herod did nothing but stay seated. And the doctrine underneath is the simplest in Scripture: my glory will I not give to another.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek demegoreo (G1215), to address a public assembly, to make an oration; skolekobrotos (G4662), eaten of worms; doxa (G1391), glory.

expand to see more

Greek demegoreo (G1215) — to harangue, to address the people; the one occurrence, Acts 12:21.

Greek skolekobrotos (G4662) — worm-eaten; he was eaten of worms.

Greek doxa (G1391) — glory, honour, praise; because he gave not God the glory.

Greek epiphoneo (G2019) — to shout out, to cry aloud; the people gave a shout.

Greek auxano (G837) — to grow, to increase; the word of God grew and multiplied.

Usage

"“sat upon his throne, and made an oration unto them” — the single occurrence."

"“because he gave not God the glory” — the stated reason for the judgment."

"“But the word of God grew and multiplied” — the sentence that follows."
